analysis.one_liner: Forgives a California farm-water district's federal repayment debt and hands it federal facilities.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee advanced the bill 23–16 in 2017, but the full House never voted and it died when Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law a 2015 settlement between the federal government and Westlands Water District, a large California irrigation district. Westlands would be let out of its obligations to repay the federal government for water-project facilities built to serve it, freed from federal rules that limit land ownership and subsidized water for large landholdings, and given title to federally built canals, pumping plants, and offices. In exchange, the federal government would end its long-unmet promise to drain salty irrigation runoff from the district's fields, leaving Westlands to manage that drainage within its own boundaries.
analysis.who_benefits: Westlands Water District and the farming operations within it. The bill would relieve Westlands of capital repayment obligations under its 1963 water service contract and 1965 repayment contract, waive federal reclamation law's land-ownership and full-cost pricing limits for Westlands lands, and transfer title to about 1,045 miles of pipeline, pumping plants, canals, and field offices [S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: A large California irrigation district and its landowners

how_it_helps.text: Westlands would be relieved of capital repayment obligations under its 1963 water service contract and any remaining obligation under its 1965 repayment contract with the United States [S3][S4].

The ownership and full-cost pricing limitations of federal reclamation law — rules meant to prevent large landholdings from receiving subsidized federal water — would not apply to lands in Westlands [S4].
The Secretary would transfer title to the San Luis Canal System distribution works, pumping plants, the drainage collection system, and field offices to Westlands [S4].
Interior would contract Central Valley Project water to Lemoore Naval Air Station, and the station's remaining repayment obligations would be discharged [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would absorb the forgiven capital repayment obligations and the non-reimbursable costs the government already incurred re-evaluating and planning drainage service for the district [S3][S4].

drawbacks.text: The bill states that the land-ownership and full-cost pricing limitations of federal reclamation law 'shall not apply to lands in Westlands' — limits designed to keep subsidized federal water from flowing to large landholdings [S4].

Westlands would be relieved of capital repayment obligations, and costs the United States incurred planning drainage service would be non-reimbursable, leaving federal taxpayers to absorb them [S3][S4].

A good-faith objection in the bill's favor: the federal government promised drainage service to these lands in 1960 and never delivered it, and decades of dispute followed; the settlement transfers both the drainage obligation and the facilities to the district, which may be cheaper than continued federal liability [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The deal would resolve a genuine decades-old dispute over drainage the government never built, and Westlands would take on real responsibility for managing drainage inside its boundaries. But the financial terms run one way: repayment obligations are forgiven, reclamation-law limits on land ownership and subsidized water for large landholders are waived, and federally built infrastructure transfers to the district. Taxpayers bear the cost while the underlying drainage problem stays the district's to handle within its own boundaries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Natural Resources Committee on a 23–16 vote and sat on the House calendar after being reported in October 2017, but the full House never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Valadao introduced the bill on March 28, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1][S6].
On April 27, 2017, the committee ordered the bill reported with amendments by a vote of 23–16 [S6].
The committee reported the bill as amended on October 16, 2017, and it was placed on the Union Calendar [S6].
The bill never received a House floor vote, the Senate never considered it, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers, who avoided having Westlands' unpaid capital obligations forgiven and the government kept title to federally built facilities — though the decades-old drainage dispute remains unresolved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers; the drainage dispute remains unresolved

industries.industry: Westlands Water District / large Central Valley farming operations
industries.note: The bill would forgive the district's capital repayment obligations under its 1963 and 1965 federal contracts, waive reclamation-law land-ownership and full-cost pricing limits, and transfer federally built canals, pumping plants, and offices to the district. The benefits flow to the district's landholdings; the costs fall on federal taxpayers.

The bill directs Interior to contract Central Valley Project water to the station and discharges its remaining repayment obligations, with shortage allocations tied to municipal and industrial contractors.
